content.title: BTS’s Comeback Show Was Heavy on Their New Album
content.text: PinnedHere’s the latest.The biggest name in K-pop is back.On Friday, the boy band and global juggernaut BTS released its first album of new music since the pandemic. On Saturday, the group performed live in central Seoul, the South Korean capital. It was their first concert in three years, five months and six days, as obsessive fans point out.The show at Gwanghwamun Square started at 8 p.m. in Seoul, or 7 a.m. in New York, and ended promptly an hour later. It was heavy on the group’s new album, “Arirang,” but also included performances of old hits like “Butter,” “Mic Drop” and “Dynamite.” They wrapped up with “Mikrokosmos,” a track from 2019.In a way, it was a grand homecoming for a pivotal force of South Korea’s soft power. The show was unusual in one sense: RM, the band’s leader, had injured his ankle and was not fully enmeshed in the ensemble. For example, during a rendition of “2.0,” a new track, he sat on a stool while the other six BTS members moved through slick dance moves.The show was streamed live by Netflix — a testament of the band’s global reach and popularity. The group’s 82-date global tour is further evidence of that appeal and also its financial heft. By some estimates the tour could rival or even surpass the $2 billion in gross ticket sales from Taylor Swift’s “Eras” outing.About 22,000 fans had tickets for the concert. The authorities expected more than a quarter of a million people to congregate in and around the square. But halfway through the show, crowd-tracking data from the Seoul government showed that there were only about 60,000 people in the area.The bandmates — RM, Jin, Jimin, V, Suga, Jungkook and J-Hope — went on hiatus in 2022 to focus on solo projects and complete their mandatory military service.“The performance was so clean,” said Kausha Campbell, 33, a dancer visiting from Los Angeles. “The military made them even cleaner and sharper.”BTS returned to a new K-pop landscape that is dominated by the Oscar and Grammy-winning film “KPop Demon Hunters,” and one that some Korean fans argue caters more to an overseas audience than its base at home.The band’s comeback paid homage to its roots. The new album’s title, “Arirang,” is the name of a Korean folk anthem symbolizing resilience and national pride. The venue of Saturday’s concert also celebrated Korean heritage: The group performed in the shadow of a sacred mountain overlooking an ancient palace and a 20-foot statue of King Sejong the Great.Here’s what we’re covering:Outfits: The band’s looks, by the Korean brand Songzio, told a broader story about Korean culture and meaning. Read more ›Promotion: The last BTS album tour kicked off with appearances in New York before Seoul. This time it’s the other way around. Read more ›Festive vibes: BTS mania took over Seoul ahead of the concert. Think lights, drones and purple pizza. Read more ›Historic setting: Gwanghwamun Square, the site of the show, near a palace of a dynasty that ruled Korea for half a millennium until 1910. Read more ›Heavy security: Officials in Seoul said there were close to 15,000 safety personnel assigned to the event. Read more ›Devoted fans: Some fans who didn’t have tickets arrived at the venue hours before to snag a good spot. Read more ›Local disruptions: The show was a headache for the neighbors. Read more ›New album: The group’s new album, “Arirang,” includes a nod to a beloved Korean folk song and other historical references. Read more ›A discography: We’ve highlighted key BTS albums and solo releases by its seven members. Read more ›Nailah Morgan and Jiawei Wang contributed reporting.March 21, 2026IN PHOTOGRAPHS AND VIDEOHere’s how BTS took over central Seoul.VideoThe historic center of Seoul has long been associated with royalty. A centuries-old palace opens into a public plaza that has large statues of two towering figures in Korean history: King Sejong the Great, who invented the Korean script, and Admiral Yi Sun-shin, who repelled Japanese invaders.On Saturday night, the plaza, Gwanghwamun Square, hosted K-pop royalty. It was the venue chosen by BTS for their comeback concert. Tens of thousands of fans sang, danced and waved light sticks to songs they knew by heart — and others that were just released on the group’s new album.Here are some images from the evening.ImageCredit...Pool photo by Kim Hong-JiOn Saturday, the group performed live in central Seoul. It was their first concert in three years, five months and six days, as obsessive fans point out.ImageCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesAbout 22,000 fans had tickets for the outdoor concert. Thousands more hovered nearby.ImageCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesBTS mania took over Seoul ahead of the concert. Some businesses were draped in purple signs, paying homage to the band’s signature color.ImageCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesThe scale of the event forced the authorities to deploy an unusually extensive array of security measures.ImageCredit...Chung Sung-Jun/Getty ImagesMany BTS fans cheered with light sticks, a staple of K-pop concerts.ImageCredit...Pool photo by Kim Hong-JiHalfway through the show, crowd-tracking data from the Seoul government showed that there were only about 60,000 people in the area. The authorities had expected as many as 260,000.ImageCredit...Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersBefore the show the band had announced that its leader, RM, had injured his ankle. But that was not obvious until he sat in a stool during the third song. Even seated, RM seemed energetic and tried to participate in choreographed moves when possible.ImageCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesAt the venue, the Seoul police rolled out security measures normally only seen at high-level government events.VideoSome fans who didn’t have tickets arrived at the venue hours before the show started, hoping to snag a good spot.VideoCreditCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesThe production required nearly six miles of power cables and screens that amounted to a total of 50 million pixels, among other equipment.ImageCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesThere was plenty of BTS merch around, of course.ImageCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesSeveral South Korean newspapers released BTS special editions on Saturday.VideoCreditCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesA department store in central Seoul drew crowds with a 3D billboard featuring the band.ImageCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesA taxi driver volunteering for traffic control wore a purple jacket, BTS style.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026Sua Son, 27, an influencer based in Turkey, said her favorite moment was when the rest of the group danced with RM. “That was a sweet moment,” she said. “It showed the teamwork and friendship they have.” She added: “It was surreal and time flew by way too fast.”ImageCredit...Yan Zhuang/The New York TimesMarch 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popThere was at least one famous fan in the crowd: Becky G. The singer-actress featured on “Chicken Noodle Soup,” a solo single by BTS member J-Hope from 2019. She has shown her support for the group over the years.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popWhile we knew RM’s ankle injury would limit his movement tonight, it was not obvious until he sat in a stool during the third song. Even seated, RM seemed energetic and tried to participate in choreographed moves when possible. Although the other six members danced away from him, the cameras included him with wide shots. So he never looked fully removed from the performance.ImageCredit...Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersMarch 21, 2026I’m the chief fashion critic at The New York Times. Yesterday I interviewed Jay Songzio, the Korean fashion designer who is responsible for all the BTS comeback concert looks, in a video call. I was really struck by the way he worked with the band to incorporate different parts of Korean history into the outfits, and by how they are using this moment to elevate all kinds of aspects of their national culture on a global stage. Here’s the interview.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popWhile saying goodbye to the crowd, V delivered one of his signature poses: a peace sign over his eyes.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popV’s influences stem partly from his love of jazz, and his velvety baritone timbre is instantly recognizable on any BTS track. He co-wrote two tracks on the new album: “2.0” and “Into the Sun.”March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popThe band members emphasize safety as they leave the stage. Jung Kook tells the crowd to have a “safe return home” before shouting that he loves them.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popJung Kook is the band’s youngest member and delivered an English-language solo album with 2023’s “Golden.” His collaborators on that album, like Diplo and Leclair, ended up working on “Arirang” as well.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popBTS closed the show with “Mikrokosmos,” a cut from 2019’s “Map of the Soul: Persona.” It’s a celestial track that the band has dedicated to its fans.March 21, 2026Jin Yu Young Reporting from the BTS concert in SeoulAnd with that, the biggest K-pop group ever has just finished its first concert in nearly four years. March 21, 2026And just in time — my fingers are about to go numb. AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026The director of the Netflix livestream is a veteran of the Oscars and the Super Bowl.ImageHamish Hamilton, an accomplished television director who specializes in live broadcasts, accepting an Emmy Award in 2024.Credit...Phil McCarten/Invision, via Associated PressIf you haven’t heard of Hamish Hamilton, you are surely familiar with at least some of his work. The multiple-Emmy-winning British director has orchestrated some of the most-viewed shows on television, including the Oscars, Olympics ceremonies and Super Bowl halftime shows.His next task? Delivering the K-pop boy band BTS’s comeback concert on Saturday from downtown Seoul to Netflix’s 325 million subscribers and the band’s global fan base.Mr. Hamilton has worked with some of the biggest names in the music industry: Beyoncé, Lady Gaga, Bruno Mars. He says BTS is as big an icon as any of them.“I genuinely believe this is every bit as significant as the Beatles arriving in America to a frenzied crowd in 1964,” Mr. Hamilton said in written responses to questions from The New York Times. “This is BTS in 2026 in Seoul; it’s going to be enormous, and I hope it makes its mark on pop-culture history.”Mr. Hamilton has been a fixture of the broadcast industry for decades. After graduating from college in the 1980s, he first worked for the BBC in Scotland. Later, while working at MTV, he developed a talent for live concert broadcasts, aiming to make the music immersive for audiences that could not be in the room, he said.His parents had envisioned a different career path for him. They wanted him to pursue accounting, he said, which he studied at the University of Stirling in Scotland. (The school awarded him an honorary doctorate in 2019 in recognition of his contributions to television producing and directing.)But music called to him. He was a student DJ in college and tried his hand at playing the bass when he was younger, he said.In 1997, Mr. Hamilton and two of his friends started a production company, Done + Dusted, to make music on television “more exciting and way more appealing,” he said in a BAFTA Special Award acceptance speech in 2013, when he won a lifetime achievement in British broadcasting.He and his friends thought the way television had portrayed music and awards shows was “pretty flat,” he said.Mr. Hamilton’s specialty is multicamera directing, a process he has described as an “alchemy of many, many different things.” He has used the method to direct some of the flashiest events in entertainment, music and sports, including 17 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Shows, three Grammys and seven Emmys.Last month, Mr. Hamilton directed the Super Bowl LX Halftime Show headlined by Bad Bunny, which attracted 128.2 million viewers, an experience he described as “simply electrifying.” He has directed every Super Bowl Halftime Show since 2010.He won an Emmy in 2023 for his work on Rihanna’s halftime show at Super Bowl LVII, and another in 2024 for directing that year’s Academy Awards. He also won a BAFTA award for the 2012 opening ceremony of the London Olympics.Despite having directed dozens of live events, Mr. Hamilton said the BTS concert would present new challenges. The group has seven members all performing complex choreography that needs to be showcased, and there would be no rehearsal on the concert stage before the night of the show.But Mr. Hamilton was confident that his team was up for the task. “Our job is to capture all of that with authenticity, intimacy and the kind of scale that does justice to the occasion,” he said.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popAfter heartfelt words to fans, BTS played their mega disco-pop hit “Dynamite.” The track was their first to top the Billboard Hot 100 and earn them a Grammy nomination. Years after its release, it’s still a major crowdpleaser — fans are chanting “encore!”VideoCreditCredit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesMarch 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popThe band took a seat onstage to perform “Like Animals” from “Arirang.” RM co-wrote the emotional rock-pop cut alongside Diplo and Artemas, the singer behind the viral hit “I Like the Way You Kiss Me.”AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026Behind the scenes of the BTS livestream.ImageGwanghwamun Square in Seoul, where the concert is taking place on Saturday.Credit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesNearly six miles of power cables. Nearly two dozen cameras. Screens that amount to a total of 50 million pixels.That’s a glimpse of what it takes to bring the BTS comeback concert in Seoul to a global audience, according to Netflix.Saturday’s show is the first time the company is streaming a music act from the Asia-Pacific region. It is also a first for Seoul. For the first time, a concert is taking over the historic Gwanghwamun Square, a public plaza in the city that sits in the shadow of a mountain.“It definitely creates different sorts of challenges,” Brandon Riegg, who oversees live programming at Netflix, said in an interview on Friday. “It’s a more public area. It’s an open-air venue.”Soon after talks began between Netflix and BTS’s management company, Hybe, he said, the group signaled that, in a perfect world, they would be able to perform at Gwanghwamun Square.The venue is public and close to other businesses, including a major concert hall that was still holding performances on Friday. Because the Netflix production team could not completely shut down the square, it had to spread out the job of building the stage and seating over a few days. On Friday morning, the production crew was still assembling the venue.Netflix crews set up what appeared to be over a dozen container offices to house different departments, including lights, audio and editing.To construct the stage, audience zones and communication networks, over 1,000 crew members from 10 countries, including the United States and Germany, have been working day and night shifts to put this together, said Sung Q Lee, Netflix’s senior director of production for the Asia-Pacific. Many of the rehearsals for lighting and LED screen displays took place at night to minimize the chance of spoilers, he said.A majority of the production crew is from South Korea, Netflix said.The crew is using cinematic cameras, like the ones used by James Cameron in “Avatar.” It is also setting up some cameras as much as a mile away from the stage while also using drone cameras, which are typically not permitted in Seoul.“This is the first time we’ve put on a show of this scale,” Mr. Lee said. March 21, 2026This is an incredibly well-behaved concert crowd and the fans with seated tickets seem to be largely staying in their seats. The cheering is not at the ear-splitting decibel I had expected. But that might be because the seating sections are so far apart that it’s hard to get a good feel for it from where we’re sitting. VideoMarch 21, 2026Why BTS is promoting its new album at home before going on tour.ImageBTS merchandise at a convenient store in Seoul on Saturday.Credit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesThe last time BTS released an album, its promotional campaign started with a conquest of the American media landscape and shifted to South Korea a few days later.Six years later, promotion for the K-pop megagroup’s latest album, “Arirang,” is running in reverse.Instead of starting in New York with an appearance on NBC’s “Today” show and a performance in Grand Central Terminal for the “Tonight Show,” as BTS did in 2020, the band is starting with a free comeback concert on Saturday in the historic center of Seoul that’s being livestreamed on Netflix.They will perform on the “Tonight Show” again, too, but not until next week.The new album takes its name from a popular Korean folk song, and the show’s setting — an outdoor stage near an ancient palace — celebrates the band’s Korean identity.Queenie Li, an associate professor of strategic communication at the University of Miami, said the focus on Korean landmarks in the Netflix trailer suggests that BTS is focused “less about going outward and more about coming back to who they are.”The album is also the group’s first since all seven members completed their mandatory military service, a rite of passage for South Korean men that is often seen as a marker of patriotism and responsibility.“‘Arirang’ ends up feeling like more than just a comeback,” Professor Li said. “It feels like a return that’s tied to identity, responsibility, and a deeper connection to their country.”The album release has also marked a return to BTS’s signature style of layered storytelling — and expanded its impact. For over a decade, fans have followed an expansive fictional “BTS Universe” across music videos, webtoons and novels. Now, BTS has teamed up with Google, Apple, Meta and other major platforms to keep fans intrigued.Before the “Arirang” release, BTS embedded references to the project through creative teasers.The group launched a Spotify scavenger hunt where fans followed digital clues to members’ voice messages, for example. And it had roses distributed in Seoul, London, and Los Angeles that included cards with QR codes that guided fans deeper into the campaign. Google hosted weeks of trivia “quests” leading up to the album release.Kim Jae-heun, a reporter in Seoul who covers K-pop for The Korea Herald Newspaper, said he saw the “Arirang” promotional campaign as one designed to target a global audience while reinforcing the band’s artistic identity.“BTS’s earlier strategy centered on establishing dominance in the U.S. during its rise,” he said, “whereas the current approach appears more measured, expansive and strategically refined.”AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popJimin, one of the group’s main vocalists, is super smiley and talkative tonight! It’s been awhile since we’ve seen him like this onstage.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popJimin co-wrote on two “Arirang” tracks: “They Don’t Know ’Bout Us” and the moving album closer, “Into the Sun.” Jimin holds the distinction as the first K-pop soloist to reach No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 when his single “Like Crazy” debuted atop the chart in 2023.March 21, 2026Jin Yu Young Reporting from the BTS concert in SeoulThe concert was advertised as free, but that wasn’t exactly the case. To be entered into a lottery for the best seats, people had to register to be part of Army, the official BTS fanbase, which came with a membership fee of 25,000 Korean won, or about $17. They also had to buy at least one copy of a packaged album set that cost 27,400 won, or about $18.ImageCredit...Chung Sung-Jun/Getty ImagesMarch 21, 2026What BTS wore for the concert and why.ImageSketches of costumes for BTS member by Korean brand Songzio.Credit...SongzioBefore BTS went on hiatus while its seven members cycled through Korean military service, they had become not just musical phenomena, but fashion phenomena. Their presence on a front row created the equivalent of millions in earned media value, and the individual members had contracts with Dior, Gucci, Calvin Klein and Celine, among other brands. For their last joint appearance at the Grammys in 2022, they wore Louis Vuitton men’s wear by Virgil Abloh.So the fact that they chose to wear looks by the Korean brand Songzio for their comeback concert was, like their choice of venue (Seoul’s historic Gwanghwamun Square) and the name of their album (“Arirang,” a 130-year-old Korean folk song), a statement as much about the place of Korean culture and identity on the global stage as about style.Songzio was founded in 1993 by Zio Song and is based in Seoul and Paris. Sold in about 120 stores worldwide, with boutiques in Seoul and Paris and one under construction in New York, the brand is designed by Jay Songzio, the 30-year-old son of the founder. It was Mr. Songzio who created the costumes for all seven BTS members and the 80 additional dancers, singers and instrumentalists involved in the concert.Here’s what he said about how it came about. This interview was edited and condensed.Were you surprised that BTS came to you for its comeback, and not one of the big European luxury names it has worked with in the past?They’ve worn our brand several times throughout their careers, but this is the first time we conceived a collection together from the very beginning. In the international luxury market, it’s difficult as an independent Korean designer. So it was heartwarming, to be honest, to have these Korean icons come to a Korean brand for this historical moment. It’s a very supportive feeling and gives me a lot of motivation.Did they explain why they wanted to work with you?They try to emphasize Korean history, but reimagine it into a more contemporary message. And that’s what we try to do ourselves — bring our Korean roots and sensibilities to our brand, but reinterpret them.ImageJay Songzio, the creative director of Songzio, left, at work.Credit...SongzioA lot of Korean history and emotion comes from this one word: Han. Han means Korea, but it can also be translated into a mix of longing and sorrow, which comes from our very turbulent and challenging history. So we tried to reimagine these BTS members as these heroic figures, leading our culture into a brighter future.Did the band have any specific design requirements?They wanted each member to have their own character. Before the army, they had more of a group identity, but now they have much, much stronger individual identities. So we had separate meetings with each member, going back and forth about what the costumes would look like.OK, so how did you imagine the characters they represent?One key word that nobody wanted for some reason was “warrior,” so I changed that to “hero.” RM is the hero, since he’s the leader. Jin is the artist. Jimin is the poet. Suga is the architect. Jungkook is the vanguard.J-Hope and V are the two characters whose names might be a bit unfamiliar. We decided to name J-Hope Sorigun. Sori means sound, and gun means men. So it’s sound men, a mix of this musical flair with history. V’s character’s name is Doryeong. There isn’t the exact word in the Western vocabulary, but it’s a mix of nobleman and sophisticated Korean gentleman.What did that mean in terms of clothing?My first idea was trying to reinterpret traditional Korean armor. But once we started designing with the different plates, it got quite rigid, which was an issue because there is a lot of activity. So we tried to mix this with hanbok, which is Korean traditional clothing, where one of the most important ideas is fluidity.ImageSongzio tried to mix traditional Korean armor with hanbok, which is Korean traditional clothing.Credit...SongzioEvery band member got one costume, but it had to transform. That was both conceptual and practical. Conceptually, it reflected the idea of metamorphosis. But they also had to perform for two, three hours, so they requested a lot of detachable elements that could be taken off, draped and worn in different ways.J-Hope has these militaristic cargo pants with a hidden zipper at knee level that could be undone to create very large volume and be worn as shorts. RM has a long jacket with a zipper that can be unzipped to create a cape-like silhouette.Was everything made in Korea?We had a lot of washed, destroyed fabrics, a lot of natural, organic fabrics, a lot of cotton and linen, all developed in Korea. We actually created a new fabric for this: a cotton hand-woven with very thick threads that kind of protrude to create a brushstroke effect like historic Korean landscape painting, which was on very rough paper.Are you going to keep working with BTS?We’re in the process of discussing the world tour. At the moment, we’re trying to reimagine the Korean flag as a group costume.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026There are about 60,000 people at Gwanghwamun Square and in the surrounding area right now, according to live crowd-tracking data from the Seoul government. City officials had predicted before the show that up to 260,000 people would be in the area tonight.ImageCredit...Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersMarch 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popAfter “Butter” and “Mic Drop,” BTS is delivering the first live performance of its new song “Aliens.” The cut is produced by Mike WiLL Made-It, the hip-hop producer who’s worked on major hits for Beyoncé, Kendrick Lamar, Rihanna, Miley Cyrus and more.March 21, 2026Jiawei WangVideo journalist reporting from the BTS concert in Seoul Sophia Baudis, a 20-year-old from Germany, came to see BTS despite a serious recent horse-riding injury, she said. She had two surgeries and is still wearing a medical boot, but she said she would travel “all over the world” to support the group’s new beginning.VideoCreditCredit...Jiawei Wang/The New York TimesMarch 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-pop“Mic Drop” is the next BTS classic for this comeback concert. Included on 2017’s “Love Yourself: Her,” the track got remixed by Steve Aoki and became an early chart hit for the group. The song spent 10 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 after peaking at No. 28.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026I’m at a theater in Bangkok, where more than 100 fans went wild when BTS started performing “Mic Drop.” Many of them have the light sticks that are a staple of K-pop concerts.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popThe song “Butter” is the first throwback of the night. Released in the spring of 2021, it was one of the band’s few original English-language singles. It topped the Billboard Hot 100 and earned the group their second Grammy nomination for best pop duo/group performance.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popWhile BTS is famous for their intense and synchronized choreography, the group began the concert embracing a more freestyled stage presence to begin the show. It’s a notable difference.March 21, 2026Jeff BenjaminMusic journalist covering K-popWe’re now seeing how RM’s ankle injury is limiting his mobility as he performed standing at a microphone stand during “Hooligan” and sits on a stool on the side of the stage during “2.0.” Of course, he’s still nailing all his lines and animated with loads of hand movements.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026“Everything is purple – my eyeshadow is purple, my hair is purple, even my heart is purple.”Ashley Bedka, 23, from Algeria and lives in SeoulImageCredit...Yan Zhuang/The New York TimesMarch 21, 2026Here’s how America met BTS.ImageMembers of BTS joined the White House press secretary, Karine Jean-Pierre, at the White House, in 2022.Credit...Doug Mills/The New York TimesWhen BTS debuted in the United States in 2014, they were greeted by thousands of screaming fans at a Korean music festival at an arena in Los Angeles.The size of that crowd is a fraction of the ones that will gather in stadiums in Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Chicago, the New York area, Toronto and Mexico City for the North American swing of their comeback tour.The sold-out shows are proof that BTS has cracked the American market, after building its fan base in the United States through television appearances and award-show performances.In 2017, BTS made the rounds on American talk shows to promote the album, “Love Yourself: Her.” The seven members danced and sang on “The Ellen DeGeneres Show,” and squeezed onto the show’s white couch for an interview with Ms. DeGeneres and a translator.When the band returned to the show in 2018, they were treated to one of her signature scares. A crew member in a blonde wig jumped out of a box, shocking J-Hope enough he fell off the couch.They were nominated for a Grammy for the first time in 2019, but did not appear onstage at the award show until 2020, when they joined the rapper Lil Nas X for a performance of his country rap hit “Old Town Road.”In 2019, they became the first K-pop group to perform on Saturday Night Live. They were introduced by the host, Emma Stone, who held her fingers up in the Korean heart gesture that BTS had helped to popularize.The band took over another New York landmark in February 2020, performing their single “ON” in an empty Grand Central Terminal for the “Tonight Show.” That same month, all seven of them piled into a van with “The Late Late Show” host James Corden for a “Carpool Karaoke” segment before crashing a dance class in Los Angeles.In 2021, they displayed their vocal chops on MTV Unplugged, forgoing their typical high-energy dance numbers for an acoustic set that included a seven-part harmonic cover of Coldplay’s “Fix You.”Before their hiatus in 2022, BTS bade farewell to their American fans with a James Bond-themed performance of “Butter” at the Grammys. In a viral moment, the American pop star Olivia Rodrigo gasped as BTS member V flirtatiously whispered into her ear, giving fans license to create memes about what he said.In a display of how deeply they had penetrated American culture, BTS were invited by former President Joe Biden to the White House in 2022 to speak about hate crimes and discrimination against Asians.“As South Korean artists and someone who witnessed transcending barriers such as languages and cultures while traveling abroad or saw our music reaching many people worldwide on tour, we wanted to talk about the power of diversity,” Suga said at the White House.Originally formed as a hip-hop band, BTS has collaborated on singles and remixes with American rappers like Snoop Dogg, Nicki Minaj and Megan Thee Stallion.Rap and hip-hop were not the only parts of American culture that have influenced the band. “My English teacher was a sitcom, ‘Friends,’” RM, the group’s leader, told Ms. DeGeneres in 2017.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026The BTS show is a headache for the neighbors.ImageGwanghwamun Square in Seoul on Saturday.Credit...Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesThe president of South Korea has personally issued instructions on concert safety and ticket scalping. At the venue, police have rolled out security measures normally only seen at high-level government events, while several nearby museums are closing for the day.Such is the gravitational pull that BTS exerts in its home country, where the group — a symbol of South Korea’s cultural export power — is ending its nearly four-year hiatus with a highly anticipated concert at Gwanghwamun Square in Seoul on Saturday.But it has disrupted the rhythms of life in the immediate neighborhood. Public transportation in the area has been suspended and access to major buildings near the venue is being blocked. Some weddings in the area are scrambling to find alternative methods of transportation for their guests. At least one couple is in talks with the Seoul police to shuttle their guests with police buses, the receptionist for the venue said.“I can’t help but question the fairness of an arrangement in which the inconvenience is borne by the public while private companies take the profits,” Kwon Yeong-guk, the head of the progressive Justice Party, said in a social media post on Thursday.The concert is expected to generate $177 million in economic impact for the city, according to an analysis by Bloomberg. To ensure the event goes off without a hitch, the authorities in Seoul have assigned around 10,000 safety personnel to the event, including more than 6,000 police officers, and another 4,800 sent by Hybe, the company that manages BTS.Officials say such extensive precautions are necessary for the safety of the 260,000 people expected to show up for the concert. But some are questioning whether the government has gone too far for what is ultimately a private production by Hybe and Netflix, which is livestreaming the concert.Baram, a human rights organization based in Seoul, said in a statement on Thursday that Seoul authorities had restricted political gatherings throughout the week in the concert area — a move it called “an abuse of governmental power.”Gwanghwamun Square has long been a cradle of political protest in Seoul, featuring regular gatherings of both far-right groups and labor unions. Protests there have drawn millions of citizens and helped depose two presidents, most recently in 2024.The Seoul chapter of a civil servants’ labor union criticized the decision to mobilize so many civil servants for the concert.“The responsibility for security at large-scale events lies primarily with the organizers,” the union said in a statement, adding that “the role of government bodies should be limited to supervision and a bare minimum of public assistance.” Mobilizing the public work force beyond that, it said, is “a misuse of administrative power.”Kim Ji-hoo, a senior official with the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency’s crisis management division, rejected the criticism that the government was catering too much to private interests.“There are so many variables with this event in terms of security. It’s such a wide-open space and there is no knowing what might happen,” he said. “Our priority is making sure that this is a safe experience for both Seoul residents and international guests.”AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTMarch 21, 2026There was extra security as BTS fans arrived at the concert site.Jun Michael Park for The New York TimesGwanghwamun Square in central Seoul, a hub of political protests, is no stranger to large crowds.
